+_SEP = 0x10FFFF # chunk separator code point (never an id below it)

+def regex_train_str(chunk_counts, num_merges, merges, vocab, verbose):
+    # unique chunks as str of code points chr(id), joined by a separator:
+    # one string per chunk weight (counts), one in chunk order (ties)
+    sep = chr(_SEP)
+    strs = list(map(bytes.decode, map(str.encode, chunk_counts),
+                    repeat("latin-1")))
+    groups = {}
+    for s, w in zip(strs, chunk_counts.values()):
+        g = groups.get(w)
+        if g is None:
+            groups[w] = [s]
+        else:
+            g.append(s)
+    order = sep.join(strs)
+    stats = {}
+    stats_get = stats.get
+    texts = []
+    for w, g in groups.items():
+        s = sep.join(g)
+        texts.append([w, s])
+        ints = list(map(ord, s))
+        if w == 1:
+            _count_elements(stats, zip(ints, ints[1:]))
+        else:
+            cnt = {}
+            _count_elements(cnt, zip(ints, ints[1:]))
+            for p, c in cnt.items():
+                stats[p] = stats_get(p, 0) + c * w
+    for p in [p for p in stats if _SEP in p]:
+        del stats[p] # pairs across chunk boundaries
+    heap = [(-c, p) for p, c in stats.items()]
+    heapify(heap)
+    for i in range(num_merges):
+        try:
+            top, tied = pop_top_pairs(heap, stats_get, heappush, heappop)
+        except ValueError:
+            max(()) # no positive count left: max()'s own error
+        pair = tied[0]
+        if len(tied) > 1:
+            # tie: earliest (chunk, position) of a first occurrence
+            best = -1
+            for p in tied:
+                j = order.find(chr(p[0]) + chr(p[1]))
+                if best < 0 or j < best:
+                    best = j
+                    pair = p
+        idx = 256 + i
+        p0, p1 = pair
+        pp = chr(p0) + chr(p1)
+        x = chr(idx)
+        order = order.replace(pp, x)
+        added = {} # new pairs contain idx: none is in stats yet
+        added_get = added.get
+        n = 0
+        for t in texts:
+            s = t[1]
+            if pp not in s:
+                continue
+            w = t[0]
+            s = t[1] = s.replace(pp, x)
+            parts = s.split(x)
+            n += (len(parts) - 1) * w
+            left = {}
+            _count_elements(left, map(_last, filter(None, parts[:-1])))
+            right = {}
+            _count_elements(right, map(_first, filter(None, parts[1:])))
+            for a, c in left.items():
+                if a != sep:
+                    a = ord(a)
+                    c *= w
+                    stats[(a, p0)] -= c
+                    p = (a, idx)
+                    added[p] = added_get(p, 0) + c
+            for b, c in right.items():
+                if b != sep:
+                    b = ord(b)
+                    c *= w
+                    stats[(p1, b)] -= c
+                    p = (idx, b)
+                    added[p] = added_get(p, 0) + c
+            c = parts[1:-1].count("")
+            if c:
+                c *= w
+                stats[(p1, p0)] -= c
+                p = (idx, idx)
+                added[p] = added_get(p, 0) + c
+        stats[pair] -= n
+        stats.update(added)
+        for p, c in added.items():
+            heappush(heap, (-c, p))

actions.reason: I tried batching RegexTokenizer training merges into C str.replace/split over weight-grouped joined chunk strings. Outputs were identical, but train_ir got worse (ratio 1.0546): splitting each whole group string on every merge costs more than the existing loop, which only touches the chunks that contain the pair. With the remaining budget I don't see another change that would reach a 1% gain on this already heavily tuned path.

journal.text:
I tried to speed up RegexTokenizer training in minbpe/_train.py by batching each merge into C-level str.replace and split calls over joined chunk strings grouped by weight, instead of the existing per-chunk Python loop. I made four edits to _train.py, touching about 110 lines in one file.

My sandbox run built cleanly and outputs were identical, but train_ir went from 312171161 to 329229820, a ratio of 1.0546, against a required 0.9900. encode_ir was flat at 1.0000. It was rejected as no improvement, and I stopped without submitting a candidate.

I now believe the existing training loop is already cheap where it matters, because it only visits chunks that contain the merged pair. Rewriting and splitting a whole group string on every merge does far more work than that targeted touch, even in C.

Next time I would keep the selective pair-to-chunk indexing and look for savings inside it, for example incremental pair count updates, rather than any whole-corpus string pass per merge.
